claim: Antigen immunogenicity and the specificity of binding of T-cell receptors to antigens are key properties underlying effective immune responses.
source: Antigen immunogenicity and the specificity of binding of T-cell receptors to antigens are key properties underlying effective immune responses.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that establishes the importance of the properties being studied, drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: DiffRBM is an approach based on transfer learning and Restricted Boltzmann Machines to build sequence-based predictive models of antigen immunogenicity and T-cell receptor specificity.
source: Here we propose diffRBM, an approach based on transfer learning and Restricted Boltzmann Machines, to build sequence-based predictive models of these properties.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the method proposed in the manuscript.

claim: The patterns learnt by diffRBM allow prediction of putative contact sites of the antigen-receptor complex.
source: We show that the patterns learnt by diffRBM allow us to predict putative contact sites of the antigen-receptor complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results presented in the manuscript showing contact prediction performance.

claim: DiffRBM can discriminate immunogenic and non-immunogenic antigens.
source: We also discriminate immunogenic and non-immunogenic antigens, antigen-specific and generic receptors, reaching performances that compare favorably to existing sequence-based predictors of antigen immunogenicity and T-cell receptor specificity.
evidence: This is supported by AUC measurements and comparisons with other methods presented in the results.

claim: DiffRBM can discriminate antigen-specific and generic receptors.
source: We also discriminate immunogenic and non-immunogenic antigens, antigen-specific and generic receptors, reaching performances that compare favorably to existing sequence-based predictors of antigen immunogenicity and T-cell receptor specificity.
evidence: This is supported by AUC measurements and comparisons with other methods presented in the results.

claim: DiffRBM reaches performances that compare favorably to existing sequence-based predictors of antigen immunogenicity and T-cell receptor specificity.
source: We also discriminate immunogenic and non-immunogenic antigens, antigen-specific and generic receptors, reaching performances that compare favorably to existing sequence-based predictors of antigen immunogenicity and T-cell receptor specificity.
evidence: This is supported by comparative performance data shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Killer T cells are activated following the binding of their surface receptors (T-cell receptors or TCRs) to short portions of pathogen-related proteins (peptide antigens) that are presented by class I major histocompatibility complexes (MHCs) forming the peptide-MHC epitope (pMHC).
source: Killer T cells are activated following the binding of their surface receptors (T-cell receptors or TCRs) to short portions of pathogen-related proteins (peptide antigens) that are presented by class I major histocompatibility complexes (MHCs) forming the peptide-MHC epitope (pMHC).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about T-cell activation.

claim: Only a fraction of peptides presented by the MHC are immunogenic.
source: Only a fraction of peptides presented by the MHC are immunogenic, meaning that they possess biochemical properties that can promote a T-cell response (Sette et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sette et al., 1994.

claim: A recent systematic assessment of available models to identify immunogenic targets from pathogens and cancers reports suboptimal overall performances.
source: A very recent systematic assessment Buckley et al., 2022 of the available models to identify immunogenic targets from pathogens and cancers reports suboptimal overall performances, with none of the models able to substantially improve beyond pure MHC-presentation prediction when evaluated on immunogenic peptides from a new virus (SARS-CoV-2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buckley et al., 2022.

claim: None of the existing models are able to substantially improve beyond pure MHC-presentation prediction when evaluated on immunogenic peptides from SARS-CoV-2.
source: A very recent systematic assessment Buckley et al., 2022 of the available models to identify immunogenic targets from pathogens and cancers reports suboptimal overall performances, with none of the models able to substantially improve beyond pure MHC-presentation prediction when evaluated on immunogenic peptides from a new virus (SARS-CoV-2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buckley et al., 2022.

claim: The largest-scale validation of existing computational pipelines for neoantigen discovery has highlighted a general lack of consensus among their predictions and a rather low average success rate, with only 6% of the predicted neoantigens validated as truly immunogenic.
source: The largest-scale validation Wells et al., 2020 of existing computational pipelines for neoantigen discovery has highlighted a general lack of consensus among their predictions and a rather low average success rate, with only 6% of the predicted neoantigens validated as truly immunogenic.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wells et al., 2020.

claim: A given pMHC epitope elicits the response of only specific small subsets of the human T-cell repertoire.
source: We also know that a given pMHC epitope elicits the response of only specific small subsets of the human T-cell repertoire.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about T-cell specificity.

claim: The model by Calis et al., 2013 is currently the most used resource for MHC class I immunogenicity prediction.
source: The model by Calis et al., 2013 is currently the most used resource for MHC class I immunogenicity prediction, being both implemented by the IEDB tool (http://tools.iedb.org/immunogenicity/) for immunogenicity predictions and integrated in the T cell-antigen interaction prediction by the NetTepi server (Trolle and Nielsen, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Calis et al., 2013 and Trolle and Nielsen, 2014.

claim: The Calis et al., 2013 model relies on measuring the enrichment in amino-acid usage between immunogenic and non-immunogenic peptides, assuming position independence of the main biophysical properties underlying immunogenicity.
source: It relies on measuring the enrichment in amino-acid usage between immunogenic and non-immunogenic peptides, assuming position independence of the main biophysical properties underlying immunogenicity.
evidence: This describes the methodology of the Calis et al., 2013 model based on the citation.

claim: Immunogenic antigens and epitope-specific receptors display an enrichment in specific patterns of amino acid composition.
source: Immunogenic antigens and epitope-specific receptors display an enrichment in specific patterns of amino acid composition.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the following sentences.

claim: Several works have shown enrichment in hydrophobic residues in immunogenic peptides, compared to all presented peptides.
source: For example, several works have shown enrichment in hydrophobic (Chowell et al., 2015; Riley et al., 2019) and aromatic (Schmidt et al., 2021) residues in immunogenic peptides, compared to all presented peptides (which are predominantly non-binders of TCRs).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chowell et al., 2015 and Riley et al., 2019.

claim: Several works have shown enrichment in aromatic residues in immunogenic peptides, compared to all presented peptides.
source: For example, several works have shown enrichment in hydrophobic (Chowell et al., 2015; Riley et al., 2019) and aromatic (Schmidt et al., 2021) residues in immunogenic peptides, compared to all presented peptides (which are predominantly non-binders of TCRs).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2021.

claim: TCRs specifically responding to the same peptide are characterized by convergent amino-acid motifs.
source: TCRs specifically responding to the same peptide are also characterized by convergent amino-acid motifs (Cinelli et al., 2017; Dash et al., 2017; Glanville et al., 2017; Pogorelyy et al., 2019a, Huang et al., 2020; Shomuradova et al., 2020; Mayer-Blackwell et al., 2021; Minervina et al., 2021; Goncharov et al., 2022), whose retrieval is the focus of several clustering approaches (Dash et al., 2017; Glanville et al., 2017; Meysman et al., 2019; Pogorelyy and Shugay, 2019b; Thakkar and Bailey-Kellogg, 2019; Mayer-Blackwell et al., 2021; Valkiers et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: DiffRBM relies on a transfer learning procedure, where general background distributions of antigen or TCR sequences are first learned, then refined to learn distinctive features that confer immunogenicity or epitope specificity.
source: DiffRBM relies on a transfer learning procedure, where we first learn general background distributions of antigen or TCR sequences, exploiting the large availability of such data. We then refine these models to learn, typically from small amounts of sequence data, the distinctive features that confer immunogenicity or epitope specificity.
evidence: This describes the methodology of diffRBM as presented in the manuscript.

claim: The parameters of background RBM are learnt from the 'background' sequence dataset.
source: The parameters of background RBM (gray) are learnt from the 'background' sequence dataset.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: The diffRBM units are learnt from a small subset of 'selected' sequences.
source: The diffRBM units (gold) are learnt from a small subset of 'selected' sequences.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: The inferred parameters associated to the diffRBM units allow identification of putative contact positions in the peptide-HLA-TCR structure.
source: The inferred parameters associated to the diffRBM units allow one to identify putative contact positions in the peptide-HLA-TCR structure (E)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and supported by results in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: DiffRBM assigns scores that distinguish the selected from the background sequences.
source: and more generally to assign scores that distinguish the selected from the background sequences (F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F and supported by results in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Immunogenic peptides were collected from the Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) for HLA-A*02:01, HLA-B*35:01, and HLA-B*07:02.
source: We collected from the Immune Epitope Database (IEDB; Vita et al., 2019) sets of peptides that elicited a T-cell reaction in T cell assays (referred to as 'immunogenic') and sets of peptides that were not T-cell-reactive ('non-immunogenic'). The peptide-presenting MHCs are specialized proteins coded by highly polymorphic human genes called Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) gene. We selected only peptides presented by 3 HLA-I alleles (HLA-A*02:01, HLA-B*35:01, HLA-B*07:02).
evidence: This describes the data collection methodology.

claim: HLA-A*02:01, HLA-B*35:01, and HLA-B*07:02 were chosen because they are associated to at least 200 immunogenic peptides in IEDB and at least one TCR-pMHC structure in the Protein Data Bank.
source: We chose these HLA-I alleles since they are associated to at least 200 immunogenic peptides in IEDB and at least one TCR-pMHC structure in the Protein Data Bank (Materials and methods).
evidence: This explains the selection criteria for the HLA alleles studied.

claim: Background RBM can predict scores of presentation on the specific HLA under consideration.
source: Background RBM can predict scores of presentation on the specific HLA under consideration, while the diffRBM units predict scores of immunogenicity.
evidence: This describes the functional capabilities of the background RBM component.

claim: The diffRBM units predict scores of immunogenicity.
source: Background RBM can predict scores of presentation on the specific HLA under consideration, while the diffRBM units predict scores of immunogenicity.
evidence: This describes the functional capabilities of the diffRBM units.

claim: Positions 2 and 9 (and 1 and 3 to a lower extent) are the anchor sites for the binding of the peptide to the HLA-I protein.
source: These contact frequency distributions highlight that positions 2 and 9 (and 1 and 3 to a lower extent) are the anchor sites for the binding of the peptide to the HLA-I protein (Figure 2B), while central positions (4-8) tend to be in contact to the TCR (Figure 2C), consistently with the analyses of structures reported in Rudolph et al., 2006; Calis et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2021; Milighetti et al., 2021.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and citations to previous structural analyses.

claim: Central positions (4-8) of peptides tend to be in contact to the TCR.
source: These contact frequency distributions highlight that positions 2 and 9 (and 1 and 3 to a lower extent) are the anchor sites for the binding of the peptide to the HLA-I protein (Figure 2B), while central positions (4-8) tend to be in contact to the TCR (Figure 2C), consistently with the analyses of structures reported in Rudolph et al., 2006; Calis et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2021; Milighetti et al., 2021.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and citations to previous structural analyses.

claim: Amino acid changes at the peptide central positions impact the most T-cell activation.
source: Previous measures of TCR functional avidity with mutant peptides indicate that amino acid changes at the peptide central positions impact the most T-cell activation (Hoof et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2021; Łuksza et al., 2022), suggesting that these positions are important for TCR response.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hoof et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2021; Łuksza et al., 2022.

claim: DiffRBM single-site factors identify positions 4–8 as the most relevant for immunogenicity in HLA-A*02:01-specific peptides.
source: Figure 2C shows the average magnitude of the diffRBM single-site factors evaluated on the 41 peptides binding to HLA-A*02:01, which identifies positions 4–8 as the most relevant for immunogenicity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The diffRBM units' prediction recovers the pattern of positions important for immunogenicity without restricting a priori the input sequences to a subset of peptide positions already known or assumed to be involved in TCR binding.
source: The diffRBM units' prediction recovers the pattern of positions important for immunogenicity without restricting a priori the input sequences to a subset of peptide positions already known or assumed to be involved in TCR binding, in contrast with existing approaches (Calis et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2021) that choose a priori what positions to retain in the formulation of the immunogenicity model.
evidence: This is a comparison with existing methods cited.

claim: The diffRBM units outperform predictions based on amino acid frequency ratios for predicting peptide-TCR contacts.
source: The diffRBM units outperform these predictions based on amino acid frequency ratios, as quantified by the average PPV (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by comparative PPV data in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The magnitude of the diffRBM single-site factors across positions correlates with the pattern of contact frequency better than predictions based on amino acid frequency ratios for HLA-A*02:01 peptides.
source: For the HLA-A*02:01 peptides, we also found that the magnitude of the diffRBM single-site factors across positions correlates with the pattern of contact frequency better than predictions based on amino acid frequency ratios (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with correlation coefficients.

claim: Immunogenic sequences show a bias towards hydrophobic amino acids, especially valine (V).
source: Some of the observed trends resemble the ones found in previous studies, for instance: the bias, in immunogenic sequences, towards hydrophobic amino acids (Chowell et al., 2015; Riley et al., 2019; Łuksza et al., 2022; Buckley et al., 2022) (especially valine, V)
evidence: This is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Immunogenic sequences show abundance of glutamic acid (E).
source: the abundance of glutamic acid (E) (Calis et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Calis et al., 2013 and data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Immunogenic sequences show moderate abundance of tryptophan (W).
source: and, to a more moderate extent, of tryptophan (W) Schmidt et al., 2021; Łuksza et al., 2022
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmidt et al., 2021; Łuksza et al., 2022 and data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Immunogenic sequences show depletion of the small polar amino acid serine (S).
source: the depletion of the small polar amino acid serine (S) and the positively charged amino acid lysine (K), consistently with the observations respectively in Chowell et al., 2015 and Schmidt et al., 2021.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chowell et al., 2015 and Schmidt et al., 2021 and data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Immunogenic sequences show depletion of the positively charged amino acid lysine (K).
source: the depletion of the small polar amino acid serine (S) and the positively charged amino acid lysine (K), consistently with the observations respectively in Chowell et al., 2015 and Schmidt et al., 2021.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chowell et al., 2015 and Schmidt et al., 2021 and data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: W at position 6 and F at position 7 were observed to form a variety of stabilizing interactions with the TCR in HLA-A*02:01 epitopes.
source: For instance, W at position 6 and F at position 7 (Schmidt et al., 2021), as well as Y at position 8 (Piepenbrink et al., 2013), were observed to form a variety of stabilizing interactions with the TCR.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmidt et al., 2021 and Piepenbrink et al., 2013.

claim: Y at position 8 was observed to form a variety of stabilizing interactions with the TCR in HLA-A*02:01 epitopes.
source: For instance, W at position 6 and F at position 7 (Schmidt et al., 2021), as well as Y at position 8 (Piepenbrink et al., 2013), were observed to form a variety of stabilizing interactions with the TCR.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Piepenbrink et al., 2013.

claim: F and W at position 5 triggered the strongest activation signal in functional avidity tests.
source: Testing functional avidity of TCRs against peptides harbouring single-point mutations, (Schmidt et al., 2021) detected that F and W at position 5 triggered the strongest activation signal
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2021.

claim: The substitution of methionine (M) at position 5 systematically abrogated TCR response.
source: while Łuksza et al., 2022 found that the substitution of methionine (M) at position 5 systematically abrogated TCR response.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Łuksza et al., 2022.

claim: For all key amino acid/position pairs (W at positions 5 and 6, F at positions 5 and 7, M at position 5, Y at position 8), the distribution of diffRBM single-site factors is skewed toward positive values.
source: For all amino acid/position pairs, the distribution of these single-site factors is skewed toward positive values (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), meaning that the diffRBM units predict a positive contribution to immunogenicity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Measuring purely the amino acid frequency ratio at key positions under the independent-site assumption predicts a contribution to immunogenicity that is significantly smaller than diffRBM predictions.
source: In contrast, measuring purely the amino acid frequency ratio at that position under the independent-site assumption predicts a contribution to immunogenicity that is significantly smaller (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B with p-values.

claim: Lethal mutations tend to occur at the typical TCR-contact positions along the peptide.
source: Lethal mutations tend to occur at the typical TCR-contact positions along the peptide (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D based on data from Łuksza et al., 2022.

claim: DiffRBM units predict mainly positive costs for lethal mutations.
source: and we confirmed that the diffRBM single-site factors predict mainly positive costs for these mutations (see Materials and methods), which matches qualitatively the observed loss of immunogenicity (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The magnitude of non-lethal mutations across all TCR-mutant pairs is concentrated at the peptide positions 2 and 9, which are the anchor sites for binding the HLA in HLA-A*02:01-specific peptides.
source: We observed that the magnitude of non-lethal mutations across all TCR-mutant pairs is concentrated at the peptide positions 2 and 9, which are the anchor sites for binding the HLA in HLA-A*02:01-specific peptides (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F based on data from Łuksza et al., 2022.

claim: The background RBM model prediction for HLA-A*02:01 presentation correlates in a statistically significant way to the experimental mutation costs for non-lethal mutations.
source: We found that the model prediction for HLA-A*02:01 presentation (background RBM) correlates in a statistically significant way to the experimental mutation costs, and the degree of correlation is consistent across all three TCRs (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B with Spearmann correlation coefficients and p-values.

claim: The diffRBM single-site factors cannot predict mutational effects concentrated at the anchor sites for presentation.
source: In contrast, the diffRBM single-site factors cannot predict these mutational effects concentrated at the anchor sites for presentation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), since its parameters capture the distinctive molecular composition of immunogenic peptides at the central positions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and explained by the model design.

claim: The AUC of discrimination progressively decreases from the diffRBM units to the full RBM to the background RBM for the HLA-A*02:01-specific model.
source: The AUC of discrimination progressively decreases, as expected, from the model part that disentangles enriched patterns from the background constraints (diffRBM units), to the full RBM capturing both, to the model fit to the background constraints only (background RBM).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Learning the background constraints that are shared by immunogenic and non-immunogenic peptides along with the sequence pattern enrichment distinctive of immunogenicity can act as a confounding factor when looking for features that characterize and distinguish immunogenic peptides.
source: This trend indicates that learning the background constraints that are shared by immunogenic and non-immunogenic peptides along with the sequence pattern enrichment distinctive of immunogenicity can act as a confounding factor when we look for the features that characterize and distinguish immunogenic peptides.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed trend in AUC values.

claim: The background model (trained on peptides probed for their binding to a given HLA-I) provides no clear signal that binding affinity to the HLA can discriminate immunogenic peptides.
source: The prediction by the background model (trained on peptides probed for their binding to a given HLA-I) provides no clear signal that already the binding affinity to the HLA can discriminate immunogenic peptides (average AUC = 0.55 for HLA-A*02:01, 0.50 for HLA-B*07:02, 0.53 for HLA-B*35:01, see Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with AUC values.

claim: NetMHCpan4.1 scores show a comparable difference in score distributions between immunogenic and non-immunogenic peptides (AUC = 0.54 for HLA-A*02:01, 0.48 for HLA-B*07:02, 0.53 for HLA-B*35:01).
source: To further check this prediction, we scored HLA-A*02:01 peptides by their binding affinity to the HLA through NetMHCpan4.1 (Reynisson et al., 2020) and found a comparable difference in score distributions between immunogenic and non-immunogenic peptides (AUC = 0.54 for HLA-A*02:01, 0.48 for HLA-B*07:02, 0.53 for HLA-B*35:01).
evidence: This is based on scoring peptides with NetMHCpan4.1.

claim: A recent large-scale mapping of killer T-cell recognition of candidate neopeptides at high HLA affinity did not find a significantly different distribution of HLA-binding NetMHCpan scores between immunogenic vs non-immunogenic neopeptides.
source: Our observation is in line with a recent large-scale mapping of killer T-cell recognition of candidate neopeptides at high HLA affinity (Kristensen et al., 2022), which did not find a significantly different distribution of HLA-binding NetMHCpan scores between immunogenic vs non-immunogenic neopeptides.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kristensen et al., 2022.

claim: Other studies have suggested that immunogenic peptides bind more strongly to the HLA compared to non-immunogenic ones, both in the case of viral epitopes and neo-epitopes.
source: Other studies, however, have suggested that immunogenic peptides bind more strongly to the HLA compared to non-immunogenic ones, both in the case of viral epitopes (Croft et al., 2019; Buckley et al., 2022) and neo-epitopes (Bjerregaard et al., 2017; Buckley et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Croft et al., 2019; Buckley et al., 2022; Bjerregaard et al., 2017.

claim: The deep classifier is trained in a supervised way while the RBM-based approach is semi-supervised because its training requires knowledge of only the antigens labelled as 'immunogenic'.
source: We emphasize that the deep classifier is trained in a supervised way (i.e. using information on the two 'labels', immunogenic and non-immunogenic) while our RBM-based approach in Figure 4 is 'semi-supervised' because its training requires knowledge of a portion of the 'labels' (the antigens labelled as 'immunogenic') only.
evidence: This describes the methodological difference between approaches.

claim: The background dataset for TCR models is a typical bulk TCRβ repertoire in normal conditions.
source: The background dataset, in this case, is meant as a typical bulk TCRβ repertoire in normal conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). In particular we take, to train background RBM, the repertoire of a hypothetical universal donor that was constructed by Isacchini et al., 2021 from the TCRβ repertoires of the large scale study Emerson et al., 2017 (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the data source for the background model.

claim: The sequence features captured by background RBM for TCRs concern germline-encoded amino acid usage related to stability and binding constraints, as well as additional biases in amino acid usage stemming from VDJ recombination and thymic selection.
source: The sequence features captured by background RBM concern germline-encoded amino acid usage related to stability and binding constraints (as is the case for the two conserved residues cysteine and phenylalanine delimiting the CDR3β region), as well as additional biases in amino acid usage stemming from VDJ recombination and thymic selection.
evidence: This describes what the background RBM captures based on biological knowledge.

claim: The diffRBM units for TCRs capture antigen-driven convergent sequence features that have been documented in connection to epitope specificity.
source: By design, these diffRBM units capture antigen-driven convergent sequence features that have been documented in connection to epitope specificity (Dash et al., 2017; Glanville et al., 2017; Meysman et al., 2019; Pogorelyy and Shugay, 2019b; Thakkar and Bailey-Kellogg, 2019; Mayer-Blackwell et al., 2021; Valkiers et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The distribution of contacts along the CDR3β positions consists of stretches of 3–5 contiguous amino acids in the central part of the CDR3 (6–8 positions from the left and right anchor).
source: Figure 5B shows the distribution of contacts along the CDR3β positions, which consists, as already observed in Glanville et al., 2017; Ostmeyer et al., 2019; Milighetti et al., 2021, of stretches of 3–5 contiguous amino acids in the central part of the CDR3 (6–8 positions from the left and right anchor).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and supported by citations.

claim: The average value of diffRBM single-site factors across CDR3β sequences concentrates on the CDR3β central positions and well correlates with the contact frequency distribution.
source: Their average value across CDR3β sequences concentrates on the CDR3β central positions and well correlates with the contact frequency distribution (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B with correlation coefficients.

claim: The predictive power of the diffRBM units for CDR3β-peptide contacts is superior to the position-specific amino acid frequency ratio between the antigen-specific and the bulk-repertoire set of receptors.
source: Similarly to the predictions for peptides (Figure 2D), the predictive power of the diffRBM units is superior to the position-specific amino acid frequency ratio between the antigen-specific and the bulk-repertoire set of receptors, and is substantially higher than the random expectation (the p-value of this difference at the first ranked position is 1.6 × 10-5, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C with PPV data and statistical testing.

claim: The AUC of discrimination for the diffRBM units is consistently higher than the one for the full RBM for all 4 epitope-specific models.
source: We observed the same trend described for the models of immunogenicity, whereby the AUC of discrimination for the diffRBM units is consistently higher than the one for the full RBM.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B-E.

claim: The background RBM for TCR models has no discrimination power, as it has no information on epitope specificity.
source: Any discrimination power is lost when using the background RBM, as it should, since it has no information on epitope specificity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B-E and is expected by design.

claim: Most methods for TCR specificity prediction are classifiers built from two sets of labeled data: positive samples containing receptors with the given specificity and negative ones containing receptors specific to other antigens.
source: Most methods for TCR specificity prediction (Gielis et al., 2019; Montemurro et al., 2021; Weber et al., 2021) are classifiers built from two sets of labeled data: the positive samples containing the receptors with the given specificity and the negative ones containing receptors specific to other antigens.
evidence: This describes existing methods based on citations.

claim: The diffRBM framework is semi-supervised, as negative samples are not needed.
source: The diffRBM framework is semi-supervised, as negative samples, whose construction is somewhat arbitrary, are not needed.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the diffRBM approach.

claim: The diffRBM approach is specific to an HLA type, contrary to existing pan-HLA predictors.
source: In the context of antigen immunogenicity modeling, the diffRBM approach is specific to an HLA type, contrary to existing pan-HLA predictors (Schmidt et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes a design choice of diffRBM compared to other methods.

claim: The HLA-specific approach has the advantage of better capturing the HLA-specific amino-acid usage associated with presentation in the background model.
source: This choice has the advantage of better capturing the HLA-specific amino-acid usage associated with presentation in the background model, and of being robust against cross-HLA imbalances in the available data (HLA-A*02:01 is much better represented than other alleles).
evidence: This is a reasoning about the advantages of the HLA-specific approach.

claim: The HLA-specific approach is robust against cross-HLA imbalances in the available data.
source: This choice has the advantage of better capturing the HLA-specific amino-acid usage associated with presentation in the background model, and of being robust against cross-HLA imbalances in the available data (HLA-A*02:01 is much better represented than other alleles).
evidence: This is a reasoning about the advantages of the HLA-specific approach.

claim: DiffRBM models predict TCRs binding to a given peptide, while other methods are predictive across potentially any peptide.
source: Similarly, our diffRBM models predict TCRs binding to a given peptide, while other methods (Springer et al., 2020; Weber et al., 2021; Milighetti et al., 2021) are predictive across potentially any peptide.
evidence: This describes a difference in scope between diffRBM and other methods.

claim: DiffRBM is tailored for data-limited situations.
source: DiffRBM is tailored for such data-limited situations, and, yet, is able to capture interactions between residues that cannot be modeled by simpler approaches (Figure 2, Figure 5, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparative performance data in multiple figures.

claim: DiffRBM is able to capture interactions between residues that cannot be modeled by simpler approaches.
source: DiffRBM is tailored for such data-limited situations, and, yet, is able to capture interactions between residues that cannot be modeled by simpler approaches (Figure 2, Figure 5, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparative performance data showing diffRBM outperforms linear/PWM approaches.

claim: DiffRBM is a generative model that can be used to produce new, putative sequences of antigens or TCRs with desired properties.
source: It can be used to produce new, putative sequences of antigens or TCRs with desired properties, testable in experimental setups, with potential applications in vaccine design and TCR engineering for therapeutic purposes.
evidence: This describes a potential application of the generative nature of the model.

claim: The probabilistic distribution encoded by diffRBM allows for estimating the diversity of the data space through its entropy.
source: The probabilistic distribution encoded by the model allows for estimating the diversity of the data space (through its entropy, Appendix 4), and the loss of diversity due to selection.
evidence: This describes a capability of the probabilistic model.

claim: The reduction in diversity due to selection appears rather modest for epitope-specific repertoires, consistently with previous analyses on epitope-specific CDR3β data, with the exception of the YLQPRTFLL-specific repertoire.
source: In the case of epitope-specific repertoires (Appendix 4—figure 1), this reduction appears rather modest, consistently with previous analyses on epitope-specific CDR3β data (Sethna et al., 2020), with the exception of the YLQPRTFLL-specific repertoire.
evidence: This is based on entropy calculations and comparison with previous work.

claim: DiffRBM is purely sequence-based.
source: DiffRBM is purely sequence-based
evidence: This describes a key characteristic of the method.

claim: Sequence-based methods are computationally faster and more broadly applicable than structure-informed methods.
source: These are computationally faster and more broadly applicable than structure-informed methods.
evidence: This is a general statement about the advantages of sequence-based methods.

claim: Structural features have been shown to be important to predict a positive T-cell response, both at the level of peptide binding to the MHC and TCR binding to the pMHC complex.
source: Structural features, such as the conformational arrangement of the peptide within the HLA binding groove and of TCR chains, have been shown to be important to predict a positive T-cell response, both at the level of peptide binding to the MHC (Riley et al., 2019) and TCR binding to the pMHC complex (Lin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Riley et al., 2019 and Lin et al., 2021.

claim: Structure-informed methods are often limited to TCR-peptide pairs of known crystal structures.
source: However, these methods are often limited to TCR-peptide pairs of known crystal structures, narrowing down the scope of applications.
evidence: This is a limitation of structure-based methods.

claim: Computational predictions of antigen immunogenicity by diffRBM can be used to propose candidate antigens for experimental validation and vaccine design.
source: Our computational predictions of antigen immunogenicity can be used to propose candidate antigens for experimental validation and vaccine design.
evidence: This is a potential application of the method.

claim: DiffRBM predictions can be used to identify potentially immunogenic neoantigens to target in immune-based cancer therapies.
source: Similarly, they can be used to identify potentially immunogenic neoantigens to target in immune-based cancer therapies, or to detect phenomena of immunoediting in cancer (Łuksza et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a potential application of the method with citation to Łuksza et al., 2022.

claim: DiffRBM may need to be re-trained on neoantigen-specific training sets for neoantigen modeling, given the substantial variation in method performance between pathogenic and cancer data.
source: To adapt diffRBM to neoantigen modeling, it may need to be re-trained on neoantigen-specific training sets (rather than on IEDB as done here), given the substantial variation in method performance and in the immunogenicity-related predicted features between pathogenic and cancer data (Buckley et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work based on citation to Buckley et al., 2022.

claim: DiffRBM assigned to HLA-A*02:01-presented neoantigens from the TESLA dataset an AUC of immunogenic vs non-immunogenic discrimination of 0.6 for the diffRBM units' scores and 0.69 for the difference of diffRBM units' scores.
source: As a preliminary assessment of diffRBM performance in a cancer setting, we assigned scores to the HLA-A*02:01-presented neoantigens from the TESLA dataset (Wells et al., 2020; 11 immunogenic and 227 non-immunogenic peptides). We obtained an AUC of immunogenic vs non-immunogenic discrimination, differing significantly from the random expectation (0.6 for the diffRBM units' scores and 0.69 for the difference of diffRBM units' scores).
evidence: This is a preliminary test on neoantigen data.

claim: DiffRBM provides a potentially general and flexible approach that can be used in analyzing directed evolution protocols and SELEX experiments.
source: Last of all, diffRBM provides a potentially general and flexible approach, which can be used in analyzing directed evolution protocols (Jäckel et al., 2008; Packer and Liu, 2015; Arnold, 2018) and SELEX experiments (Ellington and Szostak, 1990; Tuerk and Gold, 1990; Sola et al., 2020), where each round performs a selection of a subset of molecules from the previous round (the 'background').
evidence: This is a suggestion for future applications with citations.
